title: Stop sorting to check anagrams: the tally-sheet reel
caption:
"listen" and "silent": same letters? 🧩
Most people sort both words and compare. That's O(n log n).

Think Scrabble. You wouldn't alphabetize two racks of tiles. You'd keep a tally:
+1 for every tile in the first rack, −1 for every tile in the second.
Every row back at zero means the same tiles.

In code: return False if the lengths differ; counts is the tally sheet (a dict from letter to number); +1 for each letter of s, −1 for each letter of t; then every count must be 0. One pass: O(n).

Our test run on 1,000,000 letters (Python): sorted() 215 ms, Counter 55 ms. Counting took about a quarter of the time.

Warehouses reconcile stock the same way: +1 per box in, −1 per box out.

⚠️ The classic 26-slot array only covers a–z. Give it "café" and Python raises IndexError: list index out of range, while JavaScript quietly returns false. Beyond a–z, count with a hash map.
⚠️ Never compare sets: set("aacc") == set("ccac") is True, but they aren't anagrams. Counts matter.

Your turn: "aab" vs "abb". Which rows miss zero? 👇

caption:
Two pointers, the whole pattern on one card. 📌 Save this.

Sorted array + pair sum → opposite ends: l at the front, r at the back; too small moves l in, too big moves r in.
Remove / move while reading ahead → fast & slow: fast explores, slow marks the end of what you keep.
Area between two lines → move inward, always the shorter side (the taller one can never raise the minimum).
Merge two sorted lists → one pointer each: take the smaller head, then append the rest.

Targets: O(n) time with O(1) extra space; the merge is O(n+m).
⚠️ Opposite ends needs sorted data.
⚠️ Watch l < r: with l <= r the middle element can pair with itself.

title: Two pointers, as a gift card: trace reel (re-cut)
caption:
$15 gift card. Two items. Every cent. 🎁
The menu is sorted: $1 $3 $4 $5 $7 $8 $9.

Trying every pair takes 21 checks. With 1,000 items, it's 499,500.

Two pointers: put one finger on the cheapest item and one on the priciest.
Too low? Even the priciest item can't lift the cheapest one to $15, so cross the cheapest off.
Too high? The priciest item can't fit with anything that's left, so cross it off.

$1+$9, $3+$9, $4+$9, $5+$9, $7+$9 (too high), $7+$8 = $15. That's 6 checks instead of 21: O(n) time, O(1) memory.

Databases join sorted tables the same way (a merge join): one pointer per table, with no nested loop over every pair.

⚠️ It only works on sorted input. Stop when the fingers meet (`left < right`), or you'll buy the same item twice.

title: Hash Tables cheatsheet carousel (the real sheet, 9 slides)
caption:
Hash Tables: 5 patterns, and the smell that tells you which one. 📌 Save this.

O(1) average lookup turns nested scans into one pass.

Need complement / pair for a target → Value → index map
Duplicate inside a distance k → Sliding last-seen
First unique / order of appearance → Count then scan
Group by signature → Key = sorted / count tuple
Long consecutive run without sort → Set + expand ends

Targets: one-pass complement O(n) time, O(n) space; group by signature O(n·k log k) time, O(n·k) space; consecutive via set O(n) time, O(n) space.

⚠️ Hashing unhashable structures
⚠️ Average vs worst case

Which trap has cost you a test case? 👇

leetExpert, the interactive DSA course. Link in bio.
alt:
Slide 1. Cover. A leetExpert cheatsheet titled "Hash Tables", with a "Save this" tag. Tagline: "O(1) average lookup turns nested scans into one pass." Chips list what is inside: 5 smells to patterns, 5 patterns, 3 targets and 2 traps.

Slide 2. Smell to pattern. Need complement / pair for a target → Value → index map. Duplicate inside a distance k → Sliding last-seen. First unique / order of appearance → Count then scan. Group by signature → Key = sorted / count tuple. Long consecutive run without sort → Set + expand ends.

Slide 3. Pattern 1 of 5: Complement map. When: Two-sum family. As you scan, ask ‘have I seen target − x?’ Store value → index. One pass; don’t forget you cannot reuse the same index.

Slide 4. Pattern 2 of 5: Last-seen index window. When: Duplicates with distance constraint. Map value → latest index. When the gap ≤ k, you have a hit. Overwrite the index as you go.

Slide 5. Pattern 3 of 5: Count then first pass. When: First unique character / element. Frequency map first, then a stable left-to-right scan for count == 1. Order matters — maps alone lose it.

Slide 6. Pattern 4 of 5: Canonical key grouping. When: Anagrams / isomorphic buckets. Hash a sorted string or a count signature. Every member of a group shares one key — append to that list.

Slide 7. Pattern 5 of 5: Set + expand consecutive. When: Longest consecutive sequence. Put numbers in a set. Only start a run at n when n−1 is absent — then walk n+1… Length is the walk count.

Slide 8. Targets, time and extra space. One-pass complement: O(n) time, O(n) space (Average hash time). Group by signature: O(n·k log k) time, O(n·k) space (k = key length if sorting). Consecutive via set: O(n) time, O(n) space (Each run starts once). Traps. Hashing unhashable structures: Lists aren’t keys — freeze them (tuple / sorted string / joined counts) before inserting into a map. Average vs worst case: Interview answers assume average O(1). Pathological collisions exist; still state the average unless asked for worst-case structures.

title: Dynamic Programming cheatsheet carousel (the real sheet, 8 slides)
caption:
Dynamic Programming: 4 patterns, and the smell that tells you which one. 📌 Save this.

Subproblems + order — define the state before you code the loop.

Optimal among overlapping subproblems → DP table / memo
Count ways under constraints → Transition sum
Knapsack / decide take or skip → 2D then compress
Longest increasing / common subsequence → Sequence DP
Grid paths with obstacles → 2D fill from corners

Targets: 1d sequence dp O(n·T) time, O(n) space; classic knapsack O(n·W) time, O(W) space; grid path dp O(m·n) time, O(n)* space.

⚠️ Wrong iteration order
⚠️ Off-by-one base cases
⚠️ State that is not a decision point

Which trap has cost you a test case? 👇

leetExpert, the interactive DSA course. Link in bio.
alt:
Slide 1. Cover. A leetExpert cheatsheet titled "Dynamic Programming", with a "Save this" tag. Tagline: "Subproblems + order — define the state before you code the loop." Chips list what is inside: 5 smells to patterns, 4 patterns, 3 targets and 3 traps.

Slide 2. Smell to pattern. Optimal among overlapping subproblems → DP table / memo. Count ways under constraints → Transition sum. Knapsack / decide take or skip → 2D then compress. Longest increasing / common subsequence → Sequence DP. Grid paths with obstacles → 2D fill from corners.

Slide 3. Pattern 1 of 4: State then transition. When: You can name ‘best/ways ending at i’. Name dp[i] (or dp[i][j]) in words first. Write the recurrence and base cases. Only then pick loop order — code without a named state is guesswork.

Slide 4. Pattern 2 of 4: Memoised recursion. When: Sparse reachable states; natural recursive structure. Top-down: same recurrence, cache results. Great when bottom-up would fill a huge unused table. Still state the complexity of the cache size.

Slide 5. Pattern 3 of 4: Rolling space. When: dp[i] only needs dp[i−1] (or two rows). Keep one or two rolling rows after the recurrence is correct. Compressing first is how people invent off-by-one bugs.

Slide 6. Pattern 4 of 4: Decision at each step. When: Take / skip, or choose among prior endings. Write the choices explicitly (take item j, end a subsequence at i…). Transitions that ‘feel right’ without listing choices usually miss a case.

Slide 7. Targets, time and extra space. 1D sequence DP: O(n·T) time, O(n) space (T = work per state). Classic knapsack: O(n·W) time, O(W) space (After rolling). Grid path DP: O(m·n) time, O(n)* space (*rolling column/row). Traps. Wrong iteration order: Bottom-up must evaluate dependencies before dependents. Reverse a loop and you silently read stale zeroes — tests pass on tiny cases, fail on real ones. Off-by-one base cases: Empty prefix, zero capacity, and the first cell of a grid are where most DP bugs hide. Write them before the nested loops. State that is not a decision point: If dp[i] cannot decide between alternatives at i, you are missing a dimension. Adding the choice to the state is cheaper than a wrong recurrence.

title: "Next greater element" has a shape: the monotonic stack
caption:
For each number, find the first bigger number to its right: [2, 1, 5, 3]. Checking to the right of every number is O(n²).

Picture a concert 🎤: once someone tall stands in front of you, everyone shorter behind them is blocked for good. Only taller people ever matter again.

The stack keeps the numbers still waiting, biggest at the bottom:
2 arrives → push. 1 arrives → push. 5 arrives → pop 1 (answer 5), pop 2 (answer 5), push 5. 3 arrives → push. At the end, 5 and 3 keep −1.

def next_greater(nums):
    answer = [-1] * len(nums)
    stack = []                      # indexes, not values
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x:
            answer[stack.pop()] = x
        stack.append(i)
    return answer

Each index goes in once and comes out at most once: O(n). Our test run on 10,000 numbers (Python): 953 ms checking right of each vs 0.6 ms with the stack.

⚠️ The trap: store values instead of indexes, and when you pop you don't know where the answer goes. Look it up with index() and duplicates break it: [1, 1, 3] → [3, −1, −1].

title: This removes the even numbers. Or does it? (remove while iterating)
caption:
An AI wrote this in two seconds. It passes the sample test. Would you ship it? 🤔

for n in nums:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        nums.remove(n)

[1, 2, 3] → [1, 3] ✓
[2, 4, 6, 7] → [4, 7] ✗ (4 is even, and it survived)

Why: the for loop walks by position, and the position moves forward every time. remove() deletes the value and shifts everything after it one step left, so the next item lands in the slot you just checked, and the loop skips it. It's like checking tickets along a row of seats while everyone slides left under your finger.

Fix 1: don't edit the list you're reading. Build a new one:
return [n for n in nums if n % 2 != 0]

Fix 2, in place: a read pointer and a write pointer. Copy each keeper to write and move write forward. Write never passes read, so nothing unread is overwritten. Then del nums[write:].

And even the version that works (loop over a copy, remove from the original) is O(n²). Our test run on 100,000 numbers: 7,972 ms vs 4 ms for the new list.

Python raises "RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration" for a dict. Lists and JavaScript arrays just skip, silently.

title: If you see "contiguous", think window: the sliding window as an inchworm
caption:
Shortest stretch of [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3] with sum ≥ 7? Trying every start and every end is O(n²).

Picture an inchworm 🐛: the front stretches forward to grab new ground, and when it's overreached, the back pulls in. Neither end ever backs up.

2+3+1 = 6 → grab 2: 8 ✓ (length 4) → pull in: 6 → grab 4: 10 → pull in: 1+2+4 = 7 ✓ (length 3) → pull in: 6 → grab 3: 9 → pull in: 4+3 = 7 ✓ (length 2). Answer: 2.

for right in range(len(nums)):
    total += nums[right]
    while total >= target:
        best = min(best, right - left + 1)
        total -= nums[left]
        left += 1

Both pointers only move forward, so it's O(n) even with a loop inside a loop. Our test run on 10,000 numbers (Python): 848 ms checking every stretch vs 1.18 ms for the window.

⚠️ The trap: write if instead of while and the window shrinks at most once per step. It never gets tight: on this exact list it answers 4, not 2.
⚠️ It needs non-negative numbers. Target 5 on [4, −2, −3, 4, 1]: the window finds nothing, but [4, 1] works.

title: Max sum of k in a row. Looks clean. (the fixed window's missing last window)
caption:
An AI wrote this, and it passes the sample ([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], k = 3 → 9). Would you ship it? 🤔

def max_sum_k(nums, k):
    best = float("-inf")
    for i in range(len(nums) - k):
        best = max(best, sum(nums[i:i + k]))
    return best

[1, 2, 3, 9], k = 2 → 5. The answer is 12 (3 + 9).
[4, 5], k = 2 → -inf.

Count the windows: a 2-wide frame on 4 numbers fits at starts 0, 1 and 2. That's n − k + 1. range(n − k) stops one short, so the last window is never checked. Fix: + 1.

Second problem: every window is summed from scratch, which is O(n·k). Slide instead: sum the first window once, then add the number entering on the right and subtract the one leaving on the left. O(n).

title: Binary search in JavaScript. One character is wrong. (the float `mid`)
caption:
Tested on [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13]: every target found. Would you ship it? 🤔

const mid = (lo + hi) / 2;

Search [2, 4, 6, 8] for 6 → -1. But 6 is right there.

lo = 0, hi = 3 → (0 + 3) / 2 = 1.5. JavaScript doesn't round, so arr[1.5] is undefined. undefined isn't === 6 and isn't < 6, so the code falls into the last branch: hi = 0.5. It never looks at a real index again.

Why did the tests pass? On 7 numbers, lo + hi is even at every step. The bug only hides on lengths 1, 3, 7, 15…: one less than a power of two.

Python's / makes a float too, but it crashes: "TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not float". Loud beats silently wrong.

Fix: const mid = lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2);
It's always a whole index, and it never adds two huge numbers (overflow-safe in Java/C++).

title: Watch recursion go down and come back up (the call stack)
caption:
factorial(3) = 3 × 2 × 1. Here's what the computer actually does. 🥞

Think of cafeteria trays: every call sets a fresh tray on top, and you only ever work on the top one.

Down: factorial(3) waits on factorial(2), which waits on factorial(1), which waits on factorial(0). That's the base case: return 1.
Up: 1 × 1 = 1, pop. 2 × 1 = 2, pop. 3 × 2 = 6, pop. Answer: 6, four frames deep (n + 1).

def factorial(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 1          # the base case, the floor
    return n * factorial(n - 1)   # smaller problem; the multiply waits

Every frame costs memory. Python stops at 1,000: factorial(1000) raises "RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded". JavaScript allows around 10,000.

⚠️ Break the base case (step down by 2: 3 → 1 → −1 → …) and it skips 0 forever. It doesn't hang, it crashes.

title: Watch binary search throw away half
caption:
Find 9 in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13]. 📖 Do what you'd do with a paper dictionary: open the middle, keep one half, ignore the other.

mid = 7 < 9 → everything up to 7 is too small. Gone.
mid = 11 > 9 → 11 and everything after it. Gone.
mid = 9 → found, in 3 checks.

def binary_search(arr, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if arr[mid] == target: return mid
        elif arr[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1

Each check halves the range: O(log n). A million sorted numbers take at most 20 checks. A billion, 30.

⚠️ The classic bug: lo = mid instead of mid + 1. Search [1, 3] for 3: mid stays 0 and lo stays 0, forever.
⚠️ It only works on sorted data, or anything where one comparison tells you which half to drop.

title: Answer any range sum in O(1): prefix sums as an odometer
caption:
nums = [2, 4, 1, 5, 3]. What's the sum from index 1 to 3? 4 + 1 + 5 = 10.
Now answer 10,000 of those. Adding each range from scratch costs up to O(n) every time.

Think of a car's odometer: it only shows the total since the car was new. Any trip = end reading − start reading. You never re-drive the trip. 🚗

A prefix array is that odometer: 0, 2, 6, 7, 12, 15.

def build_prefix(nums):
    prefix = [0] * (len(nums) + 1)   # prefix[0] = 0, the sum of nothing
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + x
    return prefix

sum(l..r) = prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l]
1..3 → 12 − 2 = 10. 2..4 → 15 − 6 = 9. One subtraction, however wide the range.

Our test run, 10,000 queries on 100,000 numbers (Python): 4.96 s summing each range vs 6.1 ms with a prefix array, build included.

⚠️ Only for an array that doesn't change: update one value and every later total is stale.
⚠️ Off-by-one: prefix[r] − prefix[l] drops nums[r] (7 − 2 = 5, not 10).

Cycle detect (Floyd): O(n) time, O(1) space (No visited set needed). Traps. Losing the next pointer: Save curr.next before rewiring. Slide 2. Smell to pattern. All subsets / permutations → Backtracking tree. Constraint board (N-Queens…) → Place + prune. Divide structure in half → Recurse on parts. Every valid arrangement / path → Enumerate + record.

Slide 3. Pattern 1 of 4: Backtracking template. When: Enumerate valid configurations. Push a choice, recurse, pop. Record when a complete valid state is reached. Prune early when constraints break.

Slide 4. Pattern 2 of 4: Include / exclude. When: Subsets / combination sum. For subsets: branch on taking nums[i] or not, then advance i. Same tree, two edges.

Slide 5. Pattern 3 of 4: Swap permutations. When: All orderings of a sequence. For i…n, swap i with j≥i, recurse i+1, swap back. Generates each order once.

Slide 6. Pattern 4 of 4: Place + prune (constraints). When: N-Queens, Sudoku, safe placement. Check constraints before recursing, not after recording. Pruning at the placement step is what keeps board searches from degenerating into full enumeration.

Slide 7. Targets, time and extra space. Subsets: O(2ⁿ · n) time, O(n) space (Output-sensitive). Permutations: O(n! · n) time, O(n) space (Depth-n stack). Traps. Mutating shared arrays: Push a copy into the answer (or copy on record). Otherwise every result points at the same final list. Forgetting to unchoose: After recurse, undo the mutation (pop, unmark, swap back). Missing undo corrupts every sibling branch. Pruning after the record: If you record partial answers and only reject them later, you still walk the dead branches. Reject at the choice, not at the leaf.

title: Stop sorting to check anagrams: the tally-sheet reel (carousel)
caption:
"listen" and "silent": same letters? 🧩
Most people sort both words and compare. That's O(n log n).

Think Scrabble. You wouldn't alphabetize two racks of tiles. You'd keep a tally:
+1 for every tile in the first rack, −1 for every tile in the second.
Every row back at zero means the same tiles.

In code: return False if the lengths differ; counts is the tally sheet (a dict from letter to number); +1 for each letter of s, −1 for each letter of t; then every count must be 0. One pass: O(n).

Our test run on 1,000,000 letters (Python): sorted() 215 ms, Counter 55 ms. Counting took about a quarter of the time.

Warehouses reconcile stock the same way: +1 per box in, −1 per box out.

⚠️ The classic 26-slot array only covers a–z. Give it "café" and Python raises IndexError: list index out of range, while JavaScript quietly returns false. Beyond a–z, count with a hash map.
⚠️ Never compare sets: set("aacc") == set("ccac") is True, but they aren't anagrams. Counts matter.

title: The coach won't give you the answer (inside leetExpert) (carousel)
caption:
I ran a broken Two Sum on leetExpert. The coach didn't fix it. 👀

Draft: for each number, store it in a map, then check if its partner is there.
Run → 2 of 4 tests pass.

The coach names the case that broke:
"two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6) returned [0, 0]; expected [1, 2]. Open Hint 1."

title: "Next greater element" has a shape: the monotonic stack (carousel)
caption:
For each number, find the first bigger number to its right: [2, 1, 5, 3]. Checking to the right of every number is O(n²).

Picture a concert 🎤: once someone tall stands in front of you, everyone shorter behind them is blocked for good. Only taller people ever matter again.

The stack keeps the numbers still waiting, biggest at the bottom:
2 arrives → push. 1 arrives → push. 5 arrives → pop 1 (answer 5), pop 2 (answer 5), push 5. 3 arrives → push. At the end, 5 and 3 keep −1.

def next_greater(nums):
    answer = [-1] * len(nums)
    stack = []                      # indexes, not values
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x:
            answer[stack.pop()] = x
        stack.append(i)
    return answer

Each index goes in once and comes out at most once: O(n). Our test run on 10,000 numbers (Python): 953 ms checking right of each vs 0.6 ms with the stack.

⚠️ The trap: store values instead of indexes, and when you pop you don't know where the answer goes. Look it up with index() and duplicates break it: [1, 1, 3] → [3, −1, −1].

title: This removes the even numbers. Or does it? (remove while iterating) (carousel)
caption:
An AI wrote this in two seconds. It passes the sample test. Would you ship it? 🤔

for n in nums:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        nums.remove(n)

[1, 2, 3] → [1, 3] ✓
[2, 4, 6, 7] → [4, 7] ✗ (4 is even, and it survived)

Why: the for loop walks by position, and the position moves forward every time. remove() deletes the value and shifts everything after it one step left, so the next item lands in the slot you just checked, and the loop skips it. It's like checking tickets along a row of seats while everyone slides left under your finger.

Fix 1: don't edit the list you're reading. Build a new one:
return [n for n in nums if n % 2 != 0]

Fix 2, in place: a read pointer and a write pointer. Copy each keeper to write and move write forward. Write never passes read, so nothing unread is overwritten. Then del nums[write:].

And even the version that works (loop over a copy, remove from the original) is O(n²). Our test run on 100,000 numbers: 7,972 ms vs 4 ms for the new list.

Python raises "RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration" for a dict. Lists and JavaScript arrays just skip, silently.

title: Max sum of k in a row. Looks clean. (the fixed window's missing last window) (carousel)
caption:
An AI wrote this, and it passes the sample ([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], k = 3 → 9). Would you ship it? 🤔

def max_sum_k(nums, k):
    best = float("-inf")
    for i in range(len(nums) - k):

title: Watch recursion go down and come back up (the call stack) (carousel)
caption:
factorial(3) = 3 × 2 × 1. Here's what the computer actually does. 🥞

Think of cafeteria trays: every call sets a fresh tray on top, and you only ever work on the top one.

Down: factorial(3) waits on factorial(2), which waits on factorial(1), which waits on factorial(0). That's the base case: return 1.
Up: 1 × 1 = 1, pop. 2 × 1 = 2, pop. 3 × 2 = 6, pop. Answer: 6, four frames deep (n + 1).

def factorial(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 1          # the base case, the floor
    return n * factorial(n - 1)   # smaller problem; the multiply waits

Every frame costs memory. Python stops at 1,000: factorial(1000) raises "RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded". JavaScript allows around 10,000.

⚠️ Break the base case (step down by 2: 3 → 1 → −1 → …) and it skips 0 forever. It doesn't hang, it crashes.

title: Watch binary search throw away half (carousel)
caption:
Find 9 in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13]. 📖 Do what you'd do with a paper dictionary: open the middle, keep one half, ignore the other.

mid = 7 < 9 → everything up to 7 is too small. Gone.
mid = 11 > 9 → 11 and everything after it. Gone.
mid = 9 → found, in 3 checks.

def binary_search(arr, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if arr[mid] == target: return mid
        elif arr[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1

Each check halves the range: O(log n). A million sorted numbers take at most 20 checks. A billion, 30.

⚠️ The classic bug: lo = mid instead of mid + 1. Search [1, 3] for 3: mid stays 0 and lo stays 0, forever.

caption:

Now answer 10,000 of those. Adding each range from scratch costs up to O(n) every time.

Think of a car's odometer: it only shows the total since the car was new. Any trip = end reading − start reading. You never re-drive the trip. 🚗

A prefix array is that odometer: 0, 2, 6, 7, 12, 15.

def build_prefix(nums):
    prefix = [0] * (len(nums) + 1)   # prefix[0] = 0, the sum of nothing
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + x
    return prefix

sum(l..r) = prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l]
1..3 → 12 − 2 = 10. 2..4 → 15 − 6 = 9. One subtraction, however wide the range.

⚠️ Only for an array that doesn't change: update one value and every later total is stale.
⚠️ Off-by-one: prefix[r] − prefix[l] drops nums[r] (7 − 2 = 5, not 10).

title: Dynamic Arrays, Built From Scratch: appending isn't always O(1) (carousel, 7 slides)
caption:
Appending to an array isn't always O(1). Some appends copy everything.

A list sits on a fixed block of slots. When the block is full, the next append allocates a bigger one and copies every element over: that one append is O(n).

So why is append called O(1)? Because the block doubles. 1,000 appends trigger only 10 grows and 1,023 copies in total, about 1.02 per append.

Grow by 10 slots at a time instead and the same 1,000 appends cost 49,600 copies: 48 times more, and it gets worse as n grows.

That's what "O(1) amortized" means: averaged over the run, even though a single append can copy 512 elements.

Did you know which appends are the slow ones? 👇

leetExpert, the interactive DSA course. Link in bio.
alt:
Slide 1. Cover. Arrays & Dynamic Arrays. Appending to an array isn't always O(1). Most appends are one write. A few copy the whole array first.

Slide 2. The setup. A list sits on a fixed block Underneath is a plain array, the backing store. Its capacity is how many slots it has. Its length is how many are used. The memory after it may belong to something else, so it cannot simply grow in place.

Slide 3. The slow append. Full? Copy everything. Python code: def append(self, value): / if self._length == self._capacity: / self._grow() / self._store[self._length] = value / self._length += 1 / def _grow(self): / self._capacity *= 2 / new_store = [None] * self._capacity / for j in range(self._length): / new_store[j] = self._store[j] / self._store = new_store. When length == capacity, append allocates a bigger block and copies every element over. That one append is O(n).

Slide 4. How much bigger?. 1,000 appends, two policies Double the capacity: 10 grows · 1,023 copies. Add 10 slots each time: 100 grows · 49,600 copies. Same appends, 48 times the copying.

Slide 5. Why doubling wins. Copies at 1, 2, 4, 8, … A geometric series: it sums to under 2n copies across n appends. Spread over n appends, that is O(1) each. A fixed increment copies again every c appends, re-moving the same early elements. It never escapes O(n) per append.

Slide 6. The name for it. O(1) amortized Average copies per append: 1.02. The costliest single append: 512 copies. Amortized means averaged over the whole run. One append can still be O(n).

title: Strings in Memory & Immutability: += on a string in a loop (carousel, 7 slides)
caption:
Why += on a string inside a loop quietly goes quadratic.

Strings are immutable in Python and JavaScript. So result += w can't extend result: it allocates a new string and copies both halves in.

Join ["a", "b", "c", "d"] that way and you copy 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 characters. Collect the pieces in a list and join once: 4.

At 1,000 one-letter words it's 500,500 copies against 1,000. That's O(n² · L) against O(n · L).

Honesty note from the lesson: CPython and V8 often special-case += and hide this. The builder is the version whose cost you can prove.

Which one is in your codebase right now? 👇

leetExpert, the interactive DSA course. Link in bio.
alt:
Slide 1. Cover. Strings. `+=` on a string in a loop re-copies what it already built. Strings are immutable. Every `+=` builds a brand-new one.

Slide 2. The trap. It looks like one step per word Python code: def join_bad(words): / result = "" / for w in words: / result += w / return result. Strings are immutable. result += w allocates a new string of len(result) + len(w) and copies both in.

Slide 3. Count the copies. Join a, b, c, d += each time: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4: 10 character copies. Collect, then join once: 4 character copies. Every step re-copies the whole prefix it already built.

Slide 4. The fix. Collect the pieces. Join once. Python code: def join_good(words): / parts = [] / for w in words: / parts.append(w) / return "".join(parts). parts.append(w) stores a reference, not characters. "".join(parts) allocates once and copies each word once.

Slide 5. At scale. 1,000 one-letter words += in the loop: 500,500 copies · O(n² · L). Collect, then join: 1,000 copies · O(n · L). The triangular sum again: L + 2L + … + nL. The gap only widens as n grows.

Slide 6. Honesty note. Your interpreter may hide it CPython and V8 both special-case += on strings when the reference is private, often making it linear in practice. Rely on that and your cost depends on interpreter internals. The builder is the version whose cost you can *prove*.

Slide 7. Closing slide. From the course: Strings in Memory & Immutability, a lesson in Strings, in leetExpert, the interactive DSA course. Trace the copies yourself, then meet the builder pattern. leetexpert.com, link in bio.
